title: The Internet Subsidy Program Paying to Wire Empty Buildings
hook: Phone customers nationwide pay over $340,000 a year to keep a nearly-abandoned Alaska island 'wired' for slow internet — while the few people who actually live there just use Starlink.
key_points: The FCC's Universal Service Fund — paid for by fees on nearly every American's phone bill — is meant to bring affordable internet to remote communities.
On Adak, Alaska, a former Navy base town of roughly 20-77 residents, the fund pays a local company over $340,000 a year to keep 306 mostly-empty buildings wired for 1-10 Mbps service.
Reporters visited every subsidized building and found none of them had a resident actually using the service — most locals pay out of pocket for unsubsidized Starlink instead, which runs 447 Mbps.

The company, Adak Eagle Enterprises, has collected over $10 million combined from federal and state subsidy programs since 2016; a 2013 federal review found its owner paid himself an 'unreasonable' salary and spent subsidy funds on vehicles and a fishing boat.
The FCC kept paying a separate Alaska telecom company even after its owner went to federal prison for tax evasion, and did not respond to ProPublica's repeated questions about Adak.
content_html: Universal internet access sounds like an unambiguous public good — which is exactly why the Universal Service Fund, a subsidy baked into nearly every American's phone bill, exists to bring service to remote places the market wouldn't otherwise reach. ProPublica's Kyle Hopkins went to see what that money actually buys on Adak, a former Navy base island in Alaska's Bering Sea so remote it sits in its own time zone.
extra_html: Adak's Navy base closed in 1997, and the town now has somewhere between 20 and roughly 77 year-round residents, depending on whose estimate you use. Despite that, a local company called Adak Eagle Enterprises collects more than $340,000 a year in federal subsidies to keep 306 buildings — most of them empty — wired for internet running at just 1 to 10 megabits per second. Reporters checked every subsidized building and didn't find a single resident actually using the service; the people who do live on Adak mostly pay for Starlink themselves, which delivers 447 Mbps unsubsidized. Adak Eagle has drawn more than $10 million combined from federal and state subsidy programs since 2016, even though a 2013 federal review had already found its owner, Larry Mayes, paying himself a salary regulators called "unreasonable" and spending subsidy money on vehicles and a fishing boat. ProPublica notes the FCC has a pattern here — it kept funding a separate Alaska carrier even after that company's owner served federal prison time for tax evasion — and says the agency did not respond to repeated questions about Adak. (This describes the U.S. Federal Communications Commission's Universal Service Fund specifically.)

related.title: Regulatory Capture
related.hook: Who protects a city's drinking water when the industry that put it at risk is also the one the regulator was built to serve? That's the problem political scientists call regulatory capture.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: Freedom of Information
related.hook: You can't hold power to account for what you can't see. Freedom of information laws pry open the workings of government so citizens can actually check it.

flashcards.prompt: What is the FCC's Universal Service Fund supposed to do, and how is it funded?
flashcards.back_html: It's meant to bring affordable, fast internet to remote communities. It's funded by fees added to nearly every American's phone bill.

flashcards.prompt: What did ProPublica find when reporters checked the subsidized buildings on Adak Island?

choices.text: None of the buildings had a resident actually using the subsidized service
All 306 buildings were fully occupied and relying on the subsidized service
The subsidized service was faster than any alternative available

flashcards.explanation_html: Reporters visited every building the company reported serving and found zero residents using it — most locals use unsubsidized Starlink instead, which is far faster.

flashcards.prompt: What did a 2013 federal review find about how Adak Eagle Enterprises used its subsidy money?

choices.text: Its owner paid himself an 'unreasonable' salary and spent funds on vehicles and a fishing boat
It invested all funds into upgrading internet speeds for residents
It returned excess subsidy funds to the FCC voluntarily

flashcards.explanation_html: The 2013 review flagged the owner's pay and spending as disproportionate to the subsidy's purpose — years before the program kept paying out.

flashcards.prompt: How did the FCC respond to ProPublica's questions about the Adak subsidies?
flashcards.back_html: It didn't. ProPublica says it asked the FCC repeatedly and "the FCC never responded" — even as payments to the company continued.
